entry.title: fix(prs): third philologist pass on the rewritten beginner texts
entry.content:
fix(prs): third philologist pass on the rewritten beginner texts

Zero critical findings this round. All 34 present-tense verb forms in the
rewrite were checked against the conjugation engine and the lexicon and are
correct - including the ones that are right rather than lucky: نمی‌دود takes no
epenthetic ی where نمی‌گوید does, می‌پزد from the irregular پختن, and داشتن and
بودن stay bare.

Four majors fixed:

**رفتن was glossed "walk" in one text and "go" three texts earlier** - the app
contradicting itself on a band-1 verb. The Dari says "go"; the English now does
too.

**`حالا ماه نو است`** reads by default as "now it is the new moon" - ماه is
glossed "month; moon" in the app's own dictionary, and the collocation belongs
to the moon. Replaced with something unambiguous.

**`dō` for دو** was the only place in the corpus spelling a band-1 numeral
differently from its own card; the headword and both other texts say `dū`.

**نوشتن** was the outlier in its own dictionary: the headword read `neweshtan`
with `benewīs`, while every seed text and every derived form in the lexicon's
own examples use the Kabuli `nawishtan`/`nawīs`. The entry moved, not the
texts.

Minors: the possessive enclitic برادرم and the reflexive خود both fall outside
the L2 grammar list and every other text in the batch avoided them; one
time-adverb-before-من survived the earlier sweep; `تیز` does not collocate with
پوشیدن, and that sentence's را marked a definite object with three possible
antecedents; two English glosses were not English; and three sentences appeared
verbatim in two texts each, which reads as padding.

The first attempt at breaking one of those duplicates introduced زرد, which
would then have owed six appearances of its own - the ratchet caught it inside
a minute. Saying something different about the flower was the better fix.

entry.title: feat: pnpm seed says when the database holds a text content no longer…
entry.content:
feat: pnpm seed says when the database holds a text content no longer has

`seed.ts` only upserts, so a text renamed, re-levelled or deleted in content/
keeps its database row - and the row is what the app serves, so the old text
goes on being offered to learners with nothing anywhere saying it should not
be. build-seed-texts.ts now removes the stale files; this was the same blind
spot one layer down, and re-levelling 21 texts is exactly the operation that
would have exposed it.

Reported, never deleted. `user_texts.text_id` is a foreign key to this table,
so a text somebody has read cannot be removed without taking their reading
history with it - the same rule CLAUDE.md states for lexicon entries, for the
same reason.

Checked against production first: 89 seed rows, none orphaned. The warning is
the guard for next time, not a fix for now.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: report where tapping half a compound verb teaches the wrong word
entry.content:
feat: report where tapping half a compound verb teaches the wrong word

The tokenizer splits compound verbs, so each half resolves on its own. For
کار کردن that is harmless - tapping کار and being told "work" is roughly right.
For دوست داشتن it is not: a learner taps دوست in "I like this book" and the app
teaches them "friend". Seven places in the shipped corpus, listed by name.

Reported rather than fixed, because the fix is not local. Pointing both tokens
at the compound lexeme is rejected by the seed-text token check, which asserts
that a token's stored id is what `resolve(surface)` returns - and resolve,
having no sentence context, correctly returns the noun. Reconciling those is a
decision about the tokenizer, not a content repair.

The first version of this report flagged every "به من" in the corpus, because
"به منصه ظهور رساندن" is a compound verb beginning with به. Restricted to
two-word compounds: a report that cries wolf gets ignored, which is worse than
no report.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(prs): nine dictionary entries that contradicted the texts
entry.content:
fix(prs): nine dictionary entries that contradicted the texts

Each of these is reachable from a text a learner now reads, so tapping the word
told them the sentence they had just understood was wrong.

**ماندن** was glossed only "to stay, to remain". Its "to put, to place" sense
is one of the sharpest Dari/Iranian splits - Iranian Persian uses گذاشتن
exclusively - and two texts teach it while the dictionary denied it. That turned
a thing the app exists to teach into a contradiction.

**درد**'s example was `سرم درد دارد`, the exact construction the texts were
corrected away from two commits ago. The rule reached the content and not the
entry for the word the rule is about, so the app taught the rule and its
violation at the same time.

**پاک** was glossed "clean (energy/air)" with a C-level example about reducing
pollution, and an L1 text now uses it of a girl's heart. **قیمت** carried only
the noun "price", so `گوشت در بازار قیمت است` decoded as "meat is price"; its
headword also disagreed with its own example on the vowel. **سر** lacked the
prepositional sense that `سرِ میز` depends on. **دوست داشتن**'s example was
"This is a love/like", which is not a sentence. **جای**'s example
transliterated `این جای آرام است` as `īn jāy-e ārām ast` - the very ambiguity
that made `آن جای` wrong in the texts.

Two consistency repairs: **یاد** gave two different stem vowels for one verb
inside a single entry, and **گران** was transliterated `gerān` where Dari is
`girān`, now also marked as the register Afghans do not reach for first.

Senses and examples only - no id moved, nothing renumbered.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(prs): the new texts were L3 grammar wearing an L1 label
entry.content:
fix(prs): the new texts were L3 grammar wearing an L1 label

A philologist reviewed batch 2 and found, besides the Dari, something
structural I had missed: **the level spec was never checked against a seed
text, and both my batches broke it.**

`levels.json` states `maxSentenceWords`, `sentenceRange` and `freqBands` per
level. L1 allows six-word sentences, present tense, and bans subordinators
outright; L2 adds را and eight-word sentences but is still present-tense only.
Simple past, که-clauses, the subjunctive and comparatives first appear at L3.
Texts 001-037 obey all of that exactly. My 21 did not: 32 over-long sentences,
6 که-clauses, simple past throughout, a present perfect and a comparative - all
labelled L1. That is the Catalan B2-learners-handed-the-C1-course incident in
CLAUDE.md, in miniature: it renders perfectly and is invisible until measured.

All 21 are rewritten as L2 texts: present tense only, five or six sentences,
inside the word ceiling, no subordinators. They keep the words they were
written to teach, and the re-exposure they buy is unchanged in kind - 38 words
out of the backlog, L2 seen-once down from 52% to 43%.

**`checkShape` is now applied to seed texts.** It already existed and was only
ever run against generated ones. Reused rather than reimplemented, so the rule
a seed text is held to and the rule a generated text is held to cannot drift.
Length fails the build, because `text-checks.ts` says why: "a sentence past the
ceiling is not readable at the level, which is the entire point of the
ceiling". Sentence count and frequency band warn - both have violations in
content that shipped long ago, and turning those red would teach the next
person to silence the check. It immediately caught a pre-existing 16-word
sentence at L4, now split in two rather than trimmed.

**And `build:texts` deletes what it no longer builds.** The script only ever
wrote files, so re-levelling these 21 left their old JSON on disk - and a stale
built text is a real text to the app: loaded, offered to learners, counted in
every report. The corpus briefly held 131 files for 110 sources, and the
validator dutifully checked all 131.

Philologist findings applied: the که in `دل من می‌خواهد که بخوابم` was in the
script while the transliteration had already dropped it, so the two disagreed
and the learner saw a word with no sound; `من چیزی را دور خوب نمی‌بینم` was
ungrammatical twice over (a stranded adjective, and indefinite ی with definite
را); `این جای` reintroduced the `آن جای` garden path; `حال بد دارم` is an
English calque, not Kabuli; three transliterations invented an ezafe on
quantifier phrases (`gōsht-e kam` is not a constituent); `این هفته من`
reintroduced the time-adverb-before-من ambiguity; and `تیز` does not carry the
metaphor in `زندگی تیزتر می‌شود`.

Still open, reported not fixed: six lexicon entries this batch reaches whose
glosses contradict the texts - ماندن lacks its Dari "to put" sense, قیمت lacks
its adjectival "expensive", پاک is glossed "clean (energy/air)" with a C-level
example on an L1 word, درد's example still teaches the درد داشتن the texts were
corrected away from, دوست داشتن mistokenises to دوست "friend", and سر lacks its
prepositional "on top of".

entry.title: fix(prs): three of my own sentences spelled کتاب the other way
entry.content:
fix(prs): three of my own sentences spelled کتاب the other way

The lexicon headword is `ketāb` and every other seed text uses it; three
sentences in the new batch said `kitāb`, so a learner met two spellings of the
same word one text apart. Consistency with 6,466 entries beats my preference
for the more Dari-looking vowel.

I also tried normalising the other 62 beginner disagreements the same way -
sentence spelling to headword, mechanically - and backed it out. Checked in the
direction I had not thought of, it makes things worse: `shīsha` → `shishe` and
`mūsīqī` → `mōsīqī` move *toward* the Iranian pattern, because in those cases
the headword is the one that is wrong. Deciding which side is right for each of
the 62 is a philologist's convention call on the lexicon, not something to
settle with a string replace, and it stays on the open list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: texts say which grammar they exercise, and phrases cannot be lost
entry.content:
feat: texts say which grammar they exercise, and phrases cannot be lost

Two gaps the plan named, both small and both guarded rather than assumed.

**Texts carry grammar tags.** The grammar course and the reading course have
been two products sharing an app: 93 lessons on one side, 110 texts on the
other, and nothing saying which text lets a learner see a lesson in use.
`grammarPoints` on a text names the points it exercises, and validate-content
rejects a tag that names no lesson - a typo would otherwise make "read
something that uses what you just learned" return an empty list rather than an
error, so the text would simply never surface and nobody would find out.
Verified by misspelling one tag and watching the build reject it.

Only the 21 texts in this refactor are tagged. The other 89 stay untagged
deliberately: a tag nobody has written is honest, a tag somebody guessed is a
learner sent to the wrong text.

**A floor under set phrases.** People speak in chunks, not words, and the
dictionary holds 39 set phrases against 6,466 entries - 0.6%, which is why a
learner can know a thousand words and still not be able to open a
conversation. This cannot say how many a course needs, only that the number
must not fall. Phrases are the easiest entries to lose in a bulk lexicon edit,
because a multi-word headword looks like a data error to anything scanning for
words - and losing them is invisible, since every individual word survives.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(prs): 11 new L1 texts so beginner words actually come back
entry.content:
feat(prs): 11 new L1 texts so beginner words actually come back

The first authoring batch against the re-exposure backlog. 51% of beginner
words were met exactly once in the whole course, against PEDAGOGY §7's 6-12
encounters, and the words that shows up on are the ones a beginner needs most:
dōst (friend) once, nām (name) once, zan (woman) once, dukhtar (girl) once.
These eleven texts are built to bring the highest-frequency short words back.

Measured, L1: words seen exactly once 138 → 110, words reaching six or more
23 → 53. L1 and L2 together, 51% → 43% seen-once. 23 words have left the
backlog.

The guards did their job, repeatedly and unglamorously. The build rejected two
sentences outright - one used a word not in the dictionary, one had a bug in my
own generator. The re-exposure ratchet rejected the batch three times for
introducing words used only once or twice, which is the entire point: it will
not let a new text add a word it does not then teach.

A philologist reviewed the batch and found seven critical defects, all now
fixed. The batch was not safe to ship:

  - نام خواهر من زیبا است was translated "my sister's name is Zeba" while the
    app glosses زیبا as "beautiful" - the learner taps it and gets a flat
    contradiction.
  - مزه دار written with a space tokenises as مزه + دار, and دار is "gallows".
  - نمی‌تواند که is not Dari; توانستن takes a bare subjunctive, and Kabul uses
    the participle construction (تیز دویده نمی‌تواند) instead.
  - گل-e زیاد است put an ezafe between a subject and its copula.
  - آن جای for "there" teaches a form the learner will then mis-produce; آنجا
    is the free adverb.
  - پس فردا written with a space reads as پس‌فردا, "the day after tomorrow".
  - دل من می‌خواهد که is not how دل خواستن is said; it takes the enclitic.

Plus nine more: می‌آموزد means both "teach" and "learn" and read as the teacher
learning Dari; سرم گرم است idiomatically means "I'm busy"; a body part takes
درد کردن, not درد داشتن; inanimate plurals take singular agreement; three
sentences used a present-for-future Dari verb with a present English gloss;
and شب من / شب ما garden-path as ezafe in a batch that teaches ezafe as
possession.

Four transliteration slips repaired in the lexicon: سه was `se` where Dari
keeps the majhul `sē`, پنیر disagreed with its own example, and زیاد's example
carried the same subject-copula ezafe error.

**Reported, not fixed: `lx-6385` is a malformed entry.** Its headword is کالای,
the ezafe form of کالا stored as if it were the lemma, band 6, with the
ungrammatical example "این کالای است." It also duplicates `lx-1310` کالا. The
repair is a merge, and a merge retires an id that `user_words.lexeme_id`
references - a reviewed migration, not something to do in passing. The texts
use لباس instead, which is correctly entered and band 2, so no learner meets
the ghost through this batch.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(prs): re-exposure becomes a ratchet that can only tighten
entry.content:
feat(prs): re-exposure becomes a ratchet that can only tighten

PEDAGOGY §7 says a person needs to meet a word roughly 6 to 12 times before it
sticks. Measured across the beginner course: **371 of its 430 content words are
met fewer than six times, and 221 exactly once.** That is the finding that
produced this whole refactor, and the only one here that cannot be fixed in
code - the fix is rewriting texts by hand.

So this is a ratchet, not a gate. `re-exposure-backlog.json` lists the 371
words currently short. A content word that is short and *not* listed fails the
build: that is a new regression, and it is exactly what has been happening
unnoticed - the last batch of authoring added forty sentences and made the
number worse, because nothing was watching. The list may shrink and never grow,
and validate:content prints how many have been fixed since it was taken, so the
authoring has a number to move.

Verified by removing five words from the list and watching the build reject
them by name. Function words are excluded deliberately: they repeat by their
nature, and "met once and never again" only costs a learner on content words.

Delete the file and the check when it empties.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(core): texts come back, and the pronunciation crutch fades
entry.content:
feat(core): texts come back, and the pronunciation crutch fades

Two small rules that raise re-exposure without a single new sentence being
written - which matters, because 51% of beginner words are shown exactly once
and rewriting that course is a much larger job than either of these.

**Re-reading.** The app has never offered it: a text was read once and
abandoned while its words went into the review deck as isolated cards. A text
whose words are due again is the same repetition the scheduler is already
asking for, in the form this app is actually good at - and the text is already
written, so it costs nothing. Offered only after a week and only when at least
three of its words are due; sorted by how much is due rather than by age,
because the point is the words, not the nostalgia.

It is placed **before** the generation retry deliberately. The old behaviour
when nothing new was available was to ask the provider chain for more text -
five free-tier quotas shared by every learner of the deployment - while
something already written, already at the right level and now full of due words
sat there unoffered. Better teaching and cheaper at the same time.

**The Latin line fades by level.** With no audio, that line is the entire
pronunciation of the language, so it is never removed - on at L1, one tap away
at L2 and above, and the toggle still works everywhere. But left as a single
permanent switch it is also never put down, and the Afghan script never becomes
how a learner actually reads. Fading is the only mechanism a text-only app has.
An imported article has no level and is treated as advanced, not as beginner:
defaulting to "always" would hand a permanent crutch to exactly the learner who
brings their own reading.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(prs): the "what a person says" list is checked for bookishness
entry.content:
feat(prs): the "what a person says" list is checked for bookishness

`pragmaticFunctions` is the one category in the beginner spec whose members are
utterances rather than citation forms - asking a favour, declining, repairing a
misunderstanding. A formal-register word there teaches a learner to say the
written equivalent of "kindly repeat" to a friend, and with the dictionary 58%
formal, drifting that way is the default rather than a slip.

`verify-beginner-core` now resolves every member and reports any part tagged
formal or literary. Two today:

  acceptingDeclining: "امکان ندارد" uses امکان (formal)
  repair: "لطفاً تکرار کنید" uses تکرار (formal)

The audit that prompted this predicted three, naming می‌خواهم and اجازه بدهید as
well; measured against the lexicon's own tagging they are not formal, so the
prediction was partly wrong and the measurement stands.

Reported, not failed. Which register a given Kabul utterance belongs to is a
philologist's call on the lexicon's tagging, and turning a judgement about Dari
into a build failure would mean the next person to touch this file edits a
register field to get the gate green - which would leave the content worse and
the gate greener.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(prs): the app stops telling Kabul speakers their Dari is wrong
entry.content:
feat(prs): the app stops telling Kabul speakers their Dari is wrong

Dari has a formal written form and a very different Kabul spoken form, and the
dictionary is 58% formal against 1% spoken - while the tutor introduces itself
as a speaker from Kabul and learners can be sent messages by real Afghan
speakers. What makes this fixable in a text-only app is that Kabul spoken Dari
is a *written* register: Afghans type it constantly.

**The audit expected the recogniser to reject these forms. Measured, it does
something worse: it answers with a different word, silently.**

    ره   → رستن   "to escape"   (it is را, the object marker)
    بری  → بردن   "to carry"    (it is برای, "for")
    مه   → مه     "fog"         (it is من, "I")

A learner tapping one of those in a message from a real speaker gets that word
written into their review deck, and nothing anywhere looks broken. This is the
`registre` failure the repo already has a rule about, pointing at a register
rather than a part of speech.

A hand-written table of Kabuli forms now sits **between** the exact match and
the generated verb paradigms. The placement is the whole decision: above the
headwords it would rewrite words the lexicon states outright - a text about
weather must keep resolving مه as weather - and below the stemmer it would
never fire, because the stemmer already reaches a wrong answer. There is also
one productive rule, the Kabuli plural `-ا` for `-ها`, accepted only when what
is left is a noun, or it would swallow a large part of the verb paradigms.

Four forms collide with real entries - مه "fog", مو "hair", ره as a stem of
رستن, and استین, which `matchKey` folds onto آستین "sleeve". Those keep
resolving to the lexicon's own answer. All four are listed with their
reasoning and pinned by a test, so a spoken form that silently does nothing
fails the suite instead of being discovered by a learner. The استین collision
was found by that test rather than by reading the list, which is the argument
for it existing. Whether the Kabuli reading should win for those is a decision
about Dari, not about code, and it is left for a philologist.

The word sheet gains a "how Kabul says it" line where the registers actually
differ. Formal stays what a learner writes; spoken is what they can read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(core): grammar stops being an island
entry.content:
feat(core): grammar stops being an island

Ninety-three lessons and 589 written exercises, and completing a lesson marked
it done forever - no review, no repetition, nothing bringing the point back a
week later. Vocabulary has had a scheduler since the first migration; grammar
had a checkbox.

**A finished lesson now becomes a card**, on the same FSRS scheduler as
vocabulary - unchanged and shared, deliberately, because two schedulers become
two different ideas of when something is due. The card is the grammar point,
not the exercise: one lesson is one thing to remember rather than twelve. And
the question a review asks is drawn from that lesson's own written exercises,
which already exist and have already been reviewed. All 95 lessons are
reviewable this way, verified against the shipped course - so grammar review
costs **no model call at all**, where the existing "extra practice" button is a
generation against a quota shared by every learner of the deployment.

**One daily queue, not a second tab.** Grammar questions are interleaved
through the word session rather than appended: a block at the end is a block
people stop reaching, which is how grammar became an island in the first place.
And the queue works when either half is empty - grammar due with no words due
used to mean "All caught up", which would have left grammar exactly as isolated
as before, only with a scheduler behind it.

Two exclusions with reasons. `matchPairs` is never used as a daily item: it is
a whole-screen sorting task built to consolidate a lesson just taught, and in a
mixed queue it turns a ten-second item into a two-minute one. And a card whose
lesson no longer exists is skipped rather than stranding the session - the same
failure the vocabulary queue already guards against.

A missed grammar point is recorded as a mistake like any other, so practice can
lead with it. The mistake record does not care which system produced it.

Re-reading a lesson does not reset its schedule. People re-read a lesson when
they feel shaky, which is the worst possible moment to throw away what the
scheduler had learned about them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: two commands that say whether any of this works
entry.content:
feat: two commands that say whether any of this works

This repo's first rule is: measure the output, do not read the code and
conclude it works. There was no instrument. Every number in the audit behind
this refactor - 273 of 400 sentences with no pronunciation, 89 of 93 texts
reaching a learner, 221 beginner words shown exactly once - was counted by hand
with a throwaway one-liner, which is why none of them was noticed for months
while they got worse.

`pnpm report:content` is offline and prints pronunciation coverage, texts and
sentences per level, how many texts can be quizzed at all, re-exposure against
PEDAGOGY §7, register mix and the dictionary's shape. This is the command that
would have printed "231 of 358" without anyone needing to run an audit.

`pnpm report:learning` reads production and prints retention, the gap between
recognising and producing, comprehension, first-attempt exercise accuracy, how
much practice now costs nothing, and how many mistakes get resolved.
Aggregates only - never a learner's words, sentences or mistakes. Finding out
whether the method works needs no personal data.

**And it immediately corrected the commit before it.** The retention floor for
promotion was set to 0.75 an hour earlier, argued from FSRS being configured to
a 0.90 target. Run against the real deployment, retention is 54% - so that
threshold would have frozen every current learner at their level, silently,
which is exactly the class of defect the rule above is about. Two fixes: the
metric now counts only mature cards, because an aggregate over new and learning
cards (57%) is not a real quantity - those are failed often by design - and the
floor is 0.50, set from the data rather than from theory.

The 54% is itself a finding worth keeping: FSRS is scheduling for 90% and
getting 54%, on 70 mature reviews across seven learners. Far too thin to retune
a scheduler on, and written into the constant's comment as the reason it must
be revisited rather than left to calcify.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(core): levelling up needs evidence, not a word count
entry.content:
feat(core): levelling up needs evidence, not a word count

Promotion has only ever read one number: how many words are marked "known". Not
accuracy, not retention, not comprehension. A learner could accumulate the
count while forgetting most of it and be promoted into harder text on the
strength of a number that had stopped being true - and until the last few
commits, several hundred of those words were ones the placement invented and
nobody ever claimed.

Two floors, both read from evidence the app only started collecting in this
refactor. **Retention**, 0.75: FSRS here targets 0.90, so a learner doing the
work lands near 90% and clears this without noticing - it is a guard against
coasting, not a bar. **Comprehension**, 0.6: a question has four options, so
0.25 is the floor of pure guessing; 0.6 is comfortably above chance and
comfortably below "read every text perfectly". Neither applies until there are
20 reviews or 5 questions behind it, because three reviews and one quiz is not
a measurement and refusing a promotion on it would be refusing on noise.

**Absent evidence never blocks, and nobody is ever demoted.** Every learner
already mid-course has no comprehension history at all - the feature did not
exist - and holding them at their level for the app's own omission would punish
them for a change they did not make. The floors apply to the next promotion,
never to the level already held, and a failed read returns nothing rather than
a zero: the failure falls on the learner's side.

`evidenceBlocks` is separate from the promotion decision so the reason can be
shown. "Not yet" with no reason is the same dead end as having no requirement
at all - the learner cannot act on either.

One thing from the plan deliberately not done: it proposed capping the
count-based rule to one level at a time, because that count used to include
invented vocabulary. That is fixed at the source now, and capping as well would
take a real behaviour away from a genuinely advanced learner who should reach
their level in one step rather than several weeks. The existing test asserting
the multi-level jump was right, and it stands.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(core): the placement test can be retaken, and a retake destroys …
entry.content:
feat(core): the placement test can be retaken, and a retake destroys nothing

The placement ran exactly once per account, with no way back. A learner
mis-placed on their first day - by over-claiming, by under-claiming, or simply
by having learnt a lot since - was stuck there permanently.

The entry point is one line in the profile. The part that needed care is the
two seeding functions, which both used a plain upsert. `seedKnownWords` writes
`fsrs: null`, so on a retake it would have overwritten a word the learner had
been reviewing for months and erased its entire history. That could not happen
while the test ran once; it is the first thing that happens the moment a retake
exists. Both now ignore rows that already exist: a retake re-estimates the
level and can move words into review, and never resets progress.

Note for anyone porting this: `useSearchParams` fails the static prerender of
this page, and `pnpm gate` does not run `pnpm build`, so it passes green. The
retake flag is read from the window in a lazy initialiser instead, the way this
file already reads standalone mode.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(prs): philologist on the invented words, and two more checks
entry.content:
fix(prs): philologist on the invented words, and two more checks

Of the forty controls, a philologist found one real Dari word and fifteen more
that a speaker would simply *read*:

**چکور** is `chakōr`, the chukar partridge - a dictionary word with its own
entry, and it was a band-1 control, so the learner most likely to be wronged
was the one furthest along. Replaced.

Fifteen more are legible without being dictionary words, in two patterns.
**میزاک** is میز "table" plus the Kabuli diminutive -ک and reads as "little
table"; سبزوک، ترناک، همروش، شفناک، تبروش، گلپرد، رفشان are the same shape.
**فرگوش** differs from خرگوش "rabbit" only in where a dot sits; مشتراخ from
مشترک، مرغوت from مرغوب، مهتاچ from محتاج، پژوند from پیوند the same way. A
learner tapping one of those is reading, not over-claiming, and gets marked
down for knowing their own language. All sixteen replaced with the
philologist's own proposals.

Three more it could not vouch for without a native ear are dropped rather than
replaced - inventing three of my own would only move the risk somewhere I
cannot see it. 37 controls.

**Both patterns are now checks**, which is this repo's rule: a finding you only
fix comes back. The validator rejects a control that is a real headword under a
productive suffix, and one within a single edit of any band-1-to-3 headword.
The second immediately caught a seventeenth that the review had missed - وشکیل
is one letter from وکیل "lawyer". Verified by feeding both patterns back in
deliberately and watching each fail.

entry.title: feat(core): the placement test can no longer be beaten by saying yes
entry.content:
feat(core): the placement test can no longer be beaten by saying yes

Sign-up shows a grid of Dari words and asks which the learner knows. There was
nothing in it that is not a real word, so tapping everything placed you as
advanced. And the scoring made it worse: claiming 80% of a frequency band
marked the *entire* band known. Bands run past a thousand words, so even a
completely honest learner had up to 20% of every cleared band credited on no
evidence, by design - roughly 500 invented words for someone clearing the first
six. Those words never entered the review system and still counted toward
promotion.

**Forty invented words**, hand-written and mixed through the grid, rendered
identically to real entries - same two lines, same unvocalised script, because
anything distinguishable measures nothing. Tapping one cannot be knowledge, so
the share tapped is a direct measurement of over-claiming.

Hand-written rather than generated for the reason the plan gives: the failure
mode is inventing a word that turns out to be real and calling an honest
learner a liar for knowing their own language - invisible, and worse than
having no controls at all. `validate-content.ts` now proves the half a machine
can prove: no control may resolve through the app's own word engine. It
immediately caught two of my forty - نشتاب resolves to شتافتن, شورند to شوریدن
- which is the whole argument for writing the check before the content. The
list also goes to a philologist, because a 6,466-entry lexicon is not a
dictionary of the language.

**Scoring, rewritten around the same evidence.** Per-band rates are corrected
for over-claiming with the standard guessing correction for a yes/no
vocabulary test, which by construction leaves a learner who tapped no invented
word completely unaffected - this must never cost an honest learner anything,
and a test asserts it. Only bands where *every* sampled word was recognised are
credited, with every easier band also fully cleared: the gap between "80%" and
"every" is precisely the vocabulary the app used to invent. The topmost cleared
band is seeded into review instead of credited, so the app checks rather than
assumes. Above the over-claim limit nothing is seeded at all.

Simulated both learners that matter. One who taps the entire grid, invented
words included, ends at L1 with an estimate of zero and nothing added they did
not claim one at a time. An honest advanced learner is scored exactly as before
on the words they claimed, keeps their cleared bands, and loses only the
invention.

entry.title: feat(core): learners write the language, and "known" starts meaning s…
entry.content:
feat(core): learners write the language, and "known" starts meaning something

The biggest pedagogical gap in this app. Every flashcard has been recognition:
show the Dari, ask "do you remember this?", reveal the English, press Forgot or
Got it. The learner grades themselves - generously, with the answer already on
screen - and recognising a word is a different skill from producing one. The
app measured the easy one and called the result "known". There has been no
point anywhere in Darya where a learner writes a Dari word.

**The other direction.** A due card now sometimes gives the English and the
sentence they first met the word in, with the word blanked, and asks them to
write it. The prompt was already stored: tapping a word while reading saves its
sentence. Production is asked once a word is genuinely in review and has
survived two recognitions - demanding a word met ten seconds ago is a test of
the last ten seconds - and it is not asked of a lapsed word, which has just
been forgotten and is being re-learned.

**Grading is free and automatic.** `lexicon-index.ts` already expands every
verb paradigm and resolves any surface back to the entry that owns it; grading
is that resolution run backwards, so it costs nothing and covers all 6,466
entries rather than the ones somebody wrote answers for. Three verdicts, not
two: the right word in the wrong form is a correction rather than a
re-teaching, grades as remembered, and does not count as produced - so the card
keeps asking until the form is right.

Checked against the whole dictionary rather than fixtures: every headword and
every transliteration accepted, and no entry's headword accepted as the answer
to a different entry - the کار/کردن hazard, which would teach a wrong answer as
right and do it silently. Two tolerances, each verified before adding it.
Macrons come off, because nobody types `khāna` on a phone - but the vowel
quality does not, so `dust` is still refused for `dōst`, the exact flattening
the lexicon was repaired to remove. ZWNJ comes off, because it is invisible,
absent from phone keyboards and impossible to produce from tiles; folding it
merges exactly 11 pairs of headword spellings across the lexicon and every one
is the same word written two ways.

**Tiles or typing, and either script.** Letter tiles are the default at L1-L2,
typing from L3, and the switch is offered on every card at every level - a
learner with a Dari keyboard should not be held back by a default written for
one without. Latin spellings are accepted throughout: answering `khana` is
still recall, which is the part that matters.

**"Known" now needs evidence.** A word graduates only once it has been written
correctly at least once. `user_words.produced_at` and `produced_count` are
nullable and not backfilled - a word an existing learner already has at known
was graduated on self-report, and pretending otherwise would destroy the one
measurement these columns exist to make: the gap between recognising and
producing, which the app currently cannot see at all.

FSRS is untouched throughout. The interval says when a review happens; none of
this changes that, only what is asked at it.
